Subject: Went back to Bhilai

Siddharth,
I finally went home last weekend, first time in four years. Took a day off from the Pune office, got the overnight train, and walked straight to our old ground behind Sector 6.
It's a parking lot now. Painted lines where our pitch was. The paan shop where we split one cold drink is a phone repair counter. Even the neem tree we used as a stump is gone.
I stood there, a grown man of twenty-six, for twenty minutes. Then I understood something. I wasn't missing the ground. I was missing us, two boys of twelve, arguing about lbw until Mummy shouted from the balcony. That afternoon isn't anywhere I can buy a ticket to.
Mummy is fine, older, slower on the stairs. We had dinner and it was good, but not the thing I came for.
When you're back from Dubai, let's meet anyway. Some parking lot.
Manoj

"The strange part is, the house was still there. Same blue gate in Kannur, same coconut tree bent over the well. Amma sold it when I started working in Bengaluru, and I told myself it didn't matter.
In April I was nearby for a wedding, so I rang the bell. A young woman opened the door with a baby on her hip. I said, 'I grew up here,' and she let me in. So kind. But my room is a nursery now, pale yellow, with a mobile of paper fish.
I stood in the doorway and waited to feel at home. It didn't come. What I wanted was my brothers fighting over the window seat and Achan's radio in the verandah at six. Achan passed away in 2019. You can't ring a bell for that.
On the bus I cried a bit, then called both my brothers."
Aditi said it quietly, and her friend Ishita just nodded.

Paulo flew from Wellington to his mother's house in Hamilton for the long weekend. The first thing he noticed was the kitchen calendar: his arrival circled in red, the circle drawn so many times the paper had gone thin.
His bed was made with the dinosaur duvet he had outgrown at eleven. In the fridge sat three tubs of the seaweed soup his mother, Soo-ah, knew he liked, far more than one person could eat in three days.
On Saturday night he came downstairs for water and found his mother in the hallway, standing in front of his graduation photo. She wasn't doing anything. She was just looking, one finger resting on the frame. She turned, startled, and said, "Oh, you're up. Want tea?"
They drank it without talking much. On Monday, at the airport, she hugged him a beat longer than usual and said, "Call on Sundays. Even two minutes."

Jagdish had never been inside his father's bank in Kanpur, not since he was a small boy. Now twenty-four and home from Hyderabad for Holi, he went to drop off the tiffin Papa had forgotten.
Papa was at the cash counter, so the clerk at the next desk, Preeti ma'am, waved him to a chair. "You're Jagdish! Sit, sit." She tapped the glass on Papa's desk. Under it was a photo Jagdish had forgotten existed: him at the Class 10 prize day, all teeth. "He shows everyone," she said. "And at lunch he checks his phone, puts it down, checks again. We tease him that he is waiting for a call from the prime minister."
Jagdish looked at the photo, then at his father counting notes, head bent, grey at the temples. He had called maybe twice a month since January. When Papa finally came over, Jagdish said only, "Tiffin," and held it out, but his voice came out rough.

"Saurabh, you've been in Leeds two weeks, right? Okay, listen, because I did everything wrong my first year in Berlin.
I kept Pune alive in my room like a museum. Every Sunday I'd video-call Aai and Baba for two hours, and then feel empty all evening. I said no to every invite.

Aai watched the whole thing on video and kept shouting, 'Sonali, my girl, fold it tighter!'
Now I still call every Sunday, but shorter. I also play football with the office team on Thursdays. Home keeps me warm. It doesn't have to be the only fire, you know?"

I'm Pankaj, a retired man on the second floor, Block C, here in Ludhiana. Uma moved in opposite us last June, from somewhere in Tamil Nadu, I think Madurai.
The first thing I noticed was the kolam. Every morning, rice-flour patterns outside her door, even in the fog of December. My wife says she does it at six, still in her shawl.
In January she knocked on every door on our landing with steel boxes of sweet pongal. She said it was her festival and she didn't want to eat it alone. My son now asks for it by name.
Some evenings I see her on the stairs, talking fast in Tamil on a video call, laughing, sometimes quiet afterwards. I can't say what she feels then. Maybe she misses home more than she lets on.
But she also joined the colony walking group, and last Lohri she was the one feeding sticks into the bonfire, clapping along to songs she didn't know.

qa.a: Sharing her pongal and joining the walking group and the Lohri bonfire let her keep her own customs while becoming part of the colony, instead of keeping home only to herself.

qa.a: It has warmed them: his wife notices her early kolam, his son now asks for pongal by name, and Pankaj watches her with friendly interest and some care.

I'm Jahnavi. My tuition is in Chitra Aunty's flat, eight of us round her dining table. On Tuesday she held up Monu's notebook and said loudly, "Monu, this is copied. From whom?" Monu went red and pressed his lips together.
But the one I noticed was Rafiq. He sits next to me, and he isn't even Monu's best friend, just his cycle friend. He started wriggling on his chair like it was hot. He pulled his sleeves over his hands and bent so low his nose almost touched his book. When Chitra Aunty looked around, Rafiq flinched as if it was his name.
After tuition I asked him, "Why were you hiding? You didn't copy." He kicked a stone. "I know. But my face went hot. It felt like she was saying it to me." Then he went to wait for Monu at the gate.

Tanuja looked up. "Really? I thought everyone was laughing."

The gram panchayat had hired a projector for the women's cricket final, and half the village of Kherwadi sat on durries in the school ground. Indu, fifteen, squeezed between her brother Vaibhav and the old postman.
In the last over the team needed nine runs. Indu found she was gripping Vaibhav's wrist so hard he winced. Her own mouth was dry, her knees jumping. When the batter swung and the ball flew, Indu was on her feet before it landed, and so was everyone else, the postman too, his cap falling off.
"Six!" someone yelled. Two balls later, a four, and the ground exploded. Strangers hugged her. A grandmother Indu had never spoken to kissed her forehead.
Walking home under the stars, Indu's legs still trembled. "I didn't even hit the ball," she said. Vaibhav laughed. "You nearly broke my wrist hitting it."

The overnight bus from Jaipur to Delhi had no working lights and no charging point, and Suraj's phone was at thirty percent. He had meant to sleep. Instead he opened the news and found the landslide story: a school bus buried, parents digging with bare hands, a boy's shoe in the mud.
The signal kept dropping, so each video loaded in pieces, and he kept waiting, refreshing, waiting. He read every update until the battery died at two in the morning. Then he sat in the dark with his forehead on the cold window.
At the Delhi stop his friend Wasim, sleepy in the next seat, stretched. "You look like you haven't slept."
"I haven't."
"Exams?"
Suraj shook his head. He felt heavy all the way down to his feet and couldn't say why. He didn't know those people. There was nothing he could have done from a bus.

Dear Jagdish sir,
You asked how the flood interviews are going. The first week was bad. I transcribed six hours of village recordings, mothers describing water coming into their houses at night. By Friday I was waking at four with my heart racing, as if it were my house, and Ammi asked why her daughter looked so tired.
So I tried what you told me in my first month. When I feel it rising, I say it in my head: this is their fear, not mine. I can respect it without living in it. I stop after every two recordings and walk round the building once. I don't play the audio on the way home.
And I needed to do something with the feeling. One woman kept saying her children lost their school bags. So our office collected forty bags, and I packed them on Saturday. That helped more than anything.
Thank you for teaching me this.
Afreen

passage:
"When Farah lost her job in March, I lost my sleep. Isn't that strange? It was her job. But she'd call me at night crying, and after we hung up I'd lie there with my chest tight, reading every article about layoffs, doing her maths in my head. I was useless at work.
My cousin Rustam finally said, 'Kunal, bhai, are you helping her or drowning with her?' That stung, but he was right.
So I changed a few things. When she called, I'd listen properly, and afterwards I'd tell myself, this is her fear, I can hold her hand, but I don't have to hold the fear. I muted the layoff news. I stopped reading comments at night.
And on Saturdays we sat together with coffee and fixed her CV, line by line. She's got two interviews now. I still feel for her. I just don't carry it to bed."

qa.q: What did Kunal and Farah do together on Saturdays?
qa.a: On Saturdays they sat together with coffee and fixed her CV, line by line.

qa.q: Why did Rustam's question sting Kunal?
qa.a: It stung because Kunal could see he was taking on Farah's fear and losing sleep instead of actually helping her, and part of him knew it was true.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Kunal, and what did he choose afterwards?
qa.a: Rustam's question was the turning point; Kunal chose to listen fully, remind himself the fear was Farah's, mute the layoff news and help with her CV.

qa.q: How might Farah have experienced Kunal's change?
qa.a: She probably found him steadier and more useful, with someone calm to call and real help on her CV rather than someone as frightened as she was.

grounding: It shows an adult who separates Farah's fear from his own, cuts down heavy news and puts his feeling into practical help instead of carrying it silently.

subtype: Child freezes and cries at a friend's fall [Actor]
passage:
In the lane behind their Chennai flats, Harsha was trying his new cycle with training wheels. Uday, five, ran alongside, cheering. The front wheel hit a stone. Harsha tipped over and scraped his elbow.
Harsha cried. Uday stopped dead. His face crumpled and he howled, louder than Harsha, fists clenched, feet stuck to the road.
Harsha's grandfather hurried out and picked him up. Only then did Uday creep closer, still sobbing, patting the cycle seat.
At dinner Uday pushed his rice around. "Amma, is Harsha's elbow better? Can I take him my sticker?"

qa.q: What did Harsha's front wheel hit?
qa.a: The front wheel hit a stone.

qa.q: What does Uday's question at dinner show about how he felt toward Harsha?
qa.a: It shows he was still worried about Harsha and wanted to make him feel better, even though his own fright had kept him from helping at the time.

qa.q: What small step could help Uday next time a friend falls?
qa.a: Someone could teach him one simple thing to do, like running to call a grown-up, so he has an action ready when his feelings swamp him.

qa.q: How might Harsha's grandfather have seen Uday's howling?
qa.a: He might have thought at first that Uday was hurt too, and then realised the little boy was frightened and upset for Harsha.

grounding: It shows a young child who sees Harsha fall, cries loudly and cannot move, so he gives no help, though his caring is real.

subtype: Child freezes and cries at a friend's fall [Actor]
passage:
"Don't jump on the diwan!" Mummy called from the kitchen.
"We're pirates!" Kashish shouted.
Thump. Sachin was on the floor, holding his head, crying.
Kashish stood on the diwan and screamed. She didn't climb down.
Mummy ran in and held Sachin, pressing a cold cloth to his head. "Just a bump. Kashish, come here."
Kashish slid down and pressed against her.
"I didn't help," she whispered.
"You were frightened. Next time, shout for me. That's helping."
Kashish looked at Sachin. "You can have my pirate hat."

qa.q: What game were Kashish and Sachin playing?
qa.a: They were playing pirates.

qa.q: What was Kashish feeling when she whispered, 'I didn't help'?
qa.a: She felt bad and a little ashamed that she had only screamed; she cared about Sachin but her fright had stopped her from doing anything.

qa.q: Why was Mummy's answer a turning point for Kashish?
qa.a: Mummy told her she had been frightened and gave her one clear thing to do next time, shouting for help, so Kashish can act instead of freezing.

qa.q: How might Sachin feel when Kashish offers him her pirate hat?
qa.a: He would likely feel comforted, knowing Kashish cared about his bump even though she only screamed when he fell.

grounding: It shows a young child who sees Sachin fall, screams and cannot move, so no help comes from her, though her caring feeling is real.
